newsitem.title: USA: Albright pushes for chemical weapons pact approval.
newsitem.headline: Albright pushes for chemical weapons pact approval.

text.p: Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on Thursday joined an administration drive for U.S. Senate approval of a global treaty banning chemical weapons, saying that failure to ratify the pact would put the United Ststes "on the side of the thugs."
Albright, sworn in as America's first woman secretary of state a week ago, said approval of the treaty was a high-priority issue and appealed for bipartisan support.
"If we do not go along with this, we're on the side of the thugs," Albright said after a luncheon meeting with Democratic senators in the Capitol.
The Clinton administration is seeking approval of the 1993 treaty by the end of April. Failure to ratify it by then would deny the United States a role in its implementation.
Several Democratic senators at the meeting said they believed it would get the required two-thirds majority vote.

"It will be close," Sen. Joseph Biden of Delaware, senior Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, said. "I think it will pass and that there will be a very, very high price to pay for people who are against it."
The treaty has the strong support of the U.S. chemical industry, which fears that failure to ratify it would put U.S. firms at a competitive disadvantage.
Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott told reporters earlier that Republicans were considering administration proposals to advance the treaty.
"They made a number of proposals, which we are now reviewing, and we will have our response on those proposals or maybe some suggested changes," Lott said.
He said there had been a "positive" meeting on the pact on Wednesday between Republican senators and Sandy Berger, President Bill Clinton's national security adviser.
Lott has linked consideration of the treaty to the need for administration cooperation with Republicans on other security issues such as a national missile defence system.

The treaty must first overcome a hurdle in the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, whose chairman, North Carolina Republican Jesse Helms, has opposed it as being unverifiable. His spokesman said that Helms had no intention of allowing the treaty to go to the full Senate.
Some Senate critics of the pact have cited a potential adverse effect on small businesses.

Last September an official of the National Federation of Independent Business wrote to Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott, raising concerns about a red tape burden the treaty would impose on small business.
But the official, Dan Danner, vice president for federal government relations, said on Thursday the concerns had been answered to the group's satisfaction.
